lessons.title: China+1 and the ASEAN Manufacturing Boom: Vietnam, India and Indonesia

children.text: Walk through a Samsung smartphone factory complex in Bac Ninh province, north of Hanoi, and you will not find a company that has left China. You will find a company that decided not to depend on it alone. Samsung still designs its chips and sources a large share of components through China-linked supply chains, but roughly half of its global smartphone output is now assembled in Vietnam. That distinction, adding a second base rather than replacing the first, is the entire logic of China+1, and it is the strategy that turned Vietnam, India and Indonesia into the three biggest beneficiaries of the manufacturing realignment this course has been building toward since Chapter 1.

body.text: China+1 is not an exit strategy. It is a hedging strategy. Companies are not leaving China's manufacturing base, they are refusing to depend on it exclusively, and the countries that win under this strategy are the ones that can absorb the "+1" without needing to replicate everything China already does.

children.text: Vietnam's rise is built overwhelmingly on one company. Samsung is Vietnam's largest single foreign investor, running vast manufacturing complexes in Bac Ninh and Thai Nguyen provinces that together account for roughly half of Samsung's entire global smartphone production. Samsung's Vietnam exports alone run into the tens of billions of dollars a year, a figure large enough on its own to move Vietnam's national trade statistics. Apple's assembly partners, Foxconn and Luxshare among them, have layered on top of this, shifting production of AirPods, iPads and select MacBook lines to Vietnamese facilities through the 2020s.

Chapter 1 already showed the trade data behind this: Vietnam's share of total US goods imports roughly doubled between 2017 and 2023. That is Samsung, Apple's suppliers and a wide tail of smaller electronics assemblers, all executing the same hedge at once.

children.text: India: Scale, Incentives and a Component Gap

India's version of this story, covered in mechanism in Chapter 2 through the PLI schemes and returned to in far more depth in Chapter 4, rests on a different set of advantages: a domestic market large enough to justify local assembly on its own, a young and growing labour force, and direct government subsidies tied to production targets. What India has not yet built, at anywhere near China's or even Vietnam's depth, is the component ecosystem, the dense cluster of specialised suppliers making the connectors, printed circuit boards and precision parts that feed into final assembly. A large share of what an Indian-assembled phone or laptop contains still arrives as imported components, often from China itself, which is the same connector-country pattern Chapter 1 documented in the trade data: assembly moves, but not every link in the chain moves with it.

body.text: This component gap is not a flaw unique to India, Vietnam has it too, just less visibly, since its exports are dominated by a handful of very large, vertically capable companies like Samsung. It is the single biggest reason China+1 has not meant China's actual displacement from global manufacturing value chains, only a partial redistribution of the final assembly step.

children.text: Indonesia took a different route entirely, and it is worth studying separately because it points toward Chapter 5's material on critical minerals. Indonesia holds roughly a fifth of the world's known nickel reserves, a metal central to electric vehicle battery chemistry. Rather than exporting raw nickel ore, the government banned unprocessed ore exports outright, effective from January 2020, forcing any company that wanted Indonesian nickel to build processing and smelting capacity inside the country first.

The bet paid off. Chinese firms, led by the stainless steel and nickel conglomerate Tsingshan Holding Group, poured capital into vast smelting complexes such as the Morowali Industrial Park in Sulawesi. Indonesia's share of global nickel mine production rose from roughly 27% in 2018 to around 50% by 2022, an extraordinary concentration of a strategically critical mineral achieved through export policy rather than through winning a bidding war for foreign factories.

body.title: What to check before calling something "China+1"
steps: Confirm the company is adding capacity elsewhere, not simply closing Chinese operations entirely
Check whether the new location still imports key components or raw materials from China
Identify whether the shift is driven by cost, by tariff avoidance, or by a customer's political alignment requirement
Look for whether China retains the R&D, design or highest-value-add step while the new location handles lower-value assembly
Assess whether the destination country has genuine scale advantages, like Vietnam's electronics cluster or Indonesia's nickel reserves, or is simply riding the trend without a structural edge

Shallower component supplier ecosystem than China or Vietnam
World's largest nickel reserves, leveraged via export policy
Heavy reliance on Chinese capital and technical expertise to process it

body.title: Spot the true China+1 case
body.question: Which of these best describes a genuine China+1 dynamic, as opposed to something else entirely?
options: A company shuts down all Chinese manufacturing and moves 100% of production to Mexico
A company keeps its Chinese factory for the domestic Chinese market but opens a new Vietnam facility to supply US customers, still importing some components from China
A company that has never manufactured in China opens its first factory in Indonesia
A retailer switches its clothing supplier from one Chinese factory to another Chinese factory for lower cost
body.explanation: China+1 specifically means retaining a China base while adding a second location, often still linked to Chinese components or capital, to hedge geopolitical and tariff risk. Full exit, first-time entry with no prior China exposure, and switching between two Chinese suppliers are all different dynamics, not this one.

cards.definition: A corporate strategy of maintaining Chinese manufacturing while adding at least one additional country, to hedge tariff, geopolitical and single-source risk, rather than exiting China entirely.
The dense cluster of specialised local suppliers, connectors, boards, precision parts, that a manufacturing hub needs to support final assembly without importing every input.
A government policy of restricting export of a raw material to force downstream processing and value capture domestically, as Indonesia did with its 2020 nickel ore export ban.

points: China+1 means adding a second manufacturing base, not replacing China, and Samsung's Vietnam operations, roughly half its global smartphone output, are the clearest large-scale example.
Vietnam's advantage is a deep, already-built electronics assembly cluster anchored by Samsung; its main constraint is a small domestic market and continued reliance on Chinese components.
India's advantage is domestic market scale and PLI incentives; its main constraint is a shallower component supplier ecosystem than China or Vietnam have built.

Indonesia won a different way entirely, banning raw nickel ore exports from January 2020 to force smelting investment onshore, lifting its share of global nickel mine production from roughly 27% to roughly 50% by 2022.

In all three cases, China typically retains the highest-value-add step, design, R&D or key components, while the "+1" country absorbs assembly or resource processing, which is why this realignment has redistributed value chains rather than replaced China's role in them.

Before calling any corporate announcement a genuine China+1 shift, check whether China exposure is actually being reduced, or whether the new location is itself still dependent on Chinese inputs or capital.
